analysis.one_liner: Redefines full-time work as 40 hours a week for the health law's employer coverage mandate.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 11 cosponsors from both parties, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died in committee when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Affordable Care Act, large employers must offer health coverage or pay a penalty if their employees average 30 or more hours a week. This bill would redefine a full-time employee as someone averaging 40 hours a week, so employers would owe no coverage and no penalty for the many workers averaging 30 to 39 hours. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers with large numbers of part-time and near-full-time workers — retail chains, restaurants, staffing firms and other low-wage industries — would save the coverage they must offer and the penalties they owe for workers averaging 30 to 39 hours. Some workers might also see more hours offered, since employers would no longer need to cap schedules just under 30 to avoid the mandate. But workers in the 30-to-39-hour band would lose the requirement that their employer offer them coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large low-wage employers like retail chains

how_it_helps.text: Changes the tax code's definition of a full-time employee under the employer mandate from an average of 30 hours a week to 40 hours a week [S2][S3].
Adjusts the formula for counting a large employer's full-time workforce so that only workers averaging 40 or more hours count toward the coverage obligation and penalties [S2][S3].
Because employers can currently avoid the mandate by keeping workers under 30 hours, moving the line to 40 would remove the incentive to cap the hours of anyone already averaging 30 to 39 hours [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Workers averaging 30 to 39 hours a week would no longer have to be offered employer coverage; many would have to buy individual plans through the insurance exchanges — with larger federal subsidies picking up part of the cost — or go uninsured. Employers would shed that obligation, so the cost shifts from companies to workers and taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: Workers averaging 30 to 39 hours a week would lose the guarantee of an employer coverage offer; under the mandate's mechanics, their employer would owe them nothing even at 39 hours a week [S2][S3].

Some of those workers would move from employer plans to the individual exchanges or to uninsurance, shifting costs onto federal subsidies or onto the workers themselves in the form of uncovered medical bills.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades one real problem for another. The 30-hour rule does give employers a reason to cap schedules, which hurts workers who want more hours — that is the strongest case for the bill. But the fix works by releasing employers from any coverage obligation for the roughly half of the workforce that averages 30 to 39 hours, pushing those workers onto exchanges or into uninsurance. The cost lands on the same hourly workers the bill is sold as helping, and the gain lands on employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Daniel Lipinski of Illinois introduced the bill on August 2, 2013, joined by six Democratic colleagues as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill; the complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no vote [S5].
The bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the Affordable Care Act's 30-hour definition stayed in place: employers remain responsible for offering coverage to workers averaging 30 or more hours a week, and those workers keep that path to employer coverage. Employers with many 30-to-39-hour workers continue to bear the mandate's costs, while the savings the bill would have handed them never materialized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers stayed on the hook; workers kept coverage.

for.name: Daniel Lipinski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the employer mandate's full-time threshold to 40 hours.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Dave Camp (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors were split 7 Democrats and 4 Republicans, and no committee or floor vote was ever taken that could have split by party [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Large employers (50+ employees), especially retail, restaurants and staffing firms
industries.note: Raising the full-time line to 40 hours would let these employers avoid coverage offers and penalties for their 30-to-39-hour workers, their largest group of near-full-time staff. The industry's saving comes directly out of the coverage those workers would otherwise be owed.

Fewer workers would enroll in employer plans, but many 30-to-39-hour workers would shift to individual-market plans, moving customers between insurance channels rather than removing them. Insurers would keep most of the pool either way.
